title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Sonya's letter from Troitsa, which had come as an answer to Nicholas' prayer, had a cause. The old countess thought more and more about marrying Nicholas to an heiress. She knew Sonya was the main obstacle, and Sonya's life in the countess' house had grown harder and harder, especially after a letter from Nicholas told of his meeting with Princess Mary at Bogucharovo. The countess never let a chance slip to make humiliating or cruel remarks about Sonya.

But a few days before they left Moscow, moved and stirred up by everything going on around her, she called Sonya to her. Instead of reproaching her and making demands, she tearfully begged her to sacrifice herself and repay all the family had done for her by breaking off her engagement to Nicholas.
"I shan't be at peace until you promise me this."

Sonya burst into hysterical tears. Between sobs she answered that she would do anything and was ready for anything, but she made no actual promise and couldn't bring herself to decide to do what was asked. She had to sacrifice herself for the family that had raised and brought her up. Sacrificing herself for others was Sonya's habit. Her position in the house was such that only through sacrifice could she show her worth, and she was used to this and loved doing it. But in all her earlier acts of self-sacrifice she had been happily aware that they raised her in her own eyes and in others', and so made her more worthy of Nicholas, whom she loved more than anything in the world. Now they wanted her to sacrifice the very thing that was the whole reward of her self-sacrifice and the whole meaning of her life. For the first time she felt bitter toward those who had been her benefactors only to torture her the more painfully. She felt jealous of Natasha, who had never experienced anything like this, had never needed to sacrifice herself, but made others sacrifice themselves for her, and was loved by everybody all the same. And for the first time Sonya felt that her pure, quiet love for Nicholas was beginning to grow into a passionate feeling stronger than principle, virtue or religion. Under the influence of this feeling, Sonya, whose life of dependence had taught her without her meaning it to be secretive, answered the countess in vague general terms and avoided talking with her. She resolved to wait until she saw Nicholas, and then, not to set him free but on the contrary to bind him to her forever.

The bustle and terror of the Rostovs' last days in Moscow smothered the gloomy thoughts that weighed on Sonya. She was glad to escape from them into practical activity. But when she heard that Prince Andrew was in their house, then, despite her sincere pity for him and for Natasha, a joyful and superstitious feeling seized her: God did not intend her to be separated from Nicholas. She knew that Natasha loved no one but Prince Andrew and had never stopped loving him. She knew that, thrown together again in such terrible circumstances, they would fall in love with each other again, and that Nicholas would then be unable to marry Princess Mary, since they would be within the prohibited degrees of affinity. Despite all the terror of what had happened in those last days and in the first days of their journey, this feeling that Providence was stepping into her personal affairs cheered Sonya.
At the Troitsa monastery the Rostovs stopped for a whole day, their first break in the journey.

They were given three large rooms in the monastery hostelry, and Prince Andrew occupied one of them. The wounded man was much better that day, and Natasha was sitting with him. In the next room the count and countess sat talking respectfully with the prior, who was calling on them as old acquaintances and benefactors of the monastery. Sonya was there too, tormented by curiosity about what Prince Andrew and Natasha were saying. She could hear their voices through the door. The door opened and Natasha came out, looking excited. She didn't notice the monk, who had risen to greet her and was drawing back the wide sleeve of his right arm. She went straight up to Sonya and took her hand.
"Natasha, what are you doing? Come here!" said the countess.
Natasha went to the monk for his blessing, and he advised her to pray for help to God and His saint.
As soon as the prior withdrew, Natasha took her friend by the hand and led her into the empty room.

"Sonya, will he live?" she asked. "Sonya, how happy I am, and how unhappy!... Sonya, dovey, everything is as it used to be. If only he lives! He can't... because... because... of..." and Natasha burst into tears.
"Yes! I knew it! Thank God!" murmured Sonya. "He will live."

Sonya was as shaken as her friend, both by Natasha's fear and grief and by her own feelings, which she shared with no one. She kissed Natasha, sobbing, and comforted her. "If only he lives!" she thought. When they had wept, talked and wiped away their tears, the two friends went together to Prince Andrew's door. Natasha opened it carefully and peeped into the room, with Sonya beside her at the half-open door.
Prince Andrew was lying propped up on three pillows. His pale face was calm and his eyes were closed, and they could see that he was breathing evenly.
"Oh, Natasha!" Sonya suddenly almost screamed, catching her companion's arm and stepping back from the door.
"What? What is it?" asked Natasha.
"It's that, that..." said Sonya, white-faced, her lips trembling.
Natasha quietly closed the door and went with Sonya to the window, not yet understanding what Sonya was trying to tell her.
"You remember," said Sonya, with a solemn, frightened look. "You remember when I looked in the mirror for you... at Otradnoe at Christmas? Do you remember what I saw?"
"Yes, yes!" cried Natasha, opening her eyes wide. She vaguely recalled that Sonya had told her something about Prince Andrew, whom she had seen lying down.

"You remember?" Sonya went on. "I saw it then and told everybody, you and Dunyasha. I saw him lying on a bed," she said, making a gesture with her hand and lifting a finger at each detail, "and he had his eyes closed and was covered with just a pink quilt, and his hands were folded," she finished, convincing herself that the details she had just seen were exactly what she had seen in the mirror.

In fact she had seen nothing then and had simply said the first thing that came into her head. But what she had invented then seemed as real to her now as any other memory. She not only remembered what she had said then (that he turned to look at her and smiled, and was covered with something red), but was firmly convinced that she had seen and said then that he was covered with a pink quilt and that his eyes were closed.
"Yes, yes, it really was pink!" cried Natasha, who now thought she too remembered the word pink being used, and saw in this the most extraordinary and mysterious part of the prediction.
"But what does it mean?" she added thoughtfully.
"Oh, I don't know, it's all so strange," replied Sonya, clutching her head.
A few minutes later Prince Andrew rang, and Natasha went to him. Sonya, feeling unusually excited and moved, stayed at the window, thinking about how strange it all was.
That day they had a chance to send letters to the army, and the countess was writing to her son.

"Sonya!" said the countess, raising her eyes from her letter as her niece passed. "Sonya, won't you write to Nicholas?" She spoke in a soft, trembling voice, and in the weary eyes that looked over her spectacles Sonya read everything the countess meant by these words. Those eyes showed entreaty, shame at having to ask, fear of a refusal, and readiness for relentless hatred if she were refused.
Sonya went up to the countess and, kneeling, kissed her hand.
"Yes, Mamma, I will write," she said.

Sonya was softened, excited and moved by everything that had happened that day, above all by the mysterious fulfillment of her vision, which she had just witnessed. She now knew that the renewal of Natasha's relations with Prince Andrew would stop Nicholas from marrying Princess Mary. She was joyfully aware that the self-sacrificing spirit she was used to living in, and loved living in, had come back to her. So, with the joyful feeling of doing a magnanimous deed, and stopping several times as tears dimmed her velvety black eyes, she wrote the touching letter whose arrival had so amazed Nicholas.
